audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.reasoning: The classification fixed-strict penultimate (penultimate stress) rests on a 435-pp modern reference grammar by the fieldworker, held held by the project, with the deciding quotation verified verbatim at the stated pages; Sato explicitly says the rule is exceptionless and applies at word level across morpheme boundaries, matching classification fixed-strict, in the dominant set, domain=word. No better or competing stress source exists. sources.note: §2.17 gives NWNB consonant and vowel phoneme charts with a Kove (Ko.) column (p. 34-35: p t k, prenasalised b d q, v z g, s h, m n ng, l, (r); five vowels) and says 'Stress patterns in running speech have not been worked out in detail for most of the languages, but for words pronounced in isolation, stress is usually penultimate in all languages.' No mention of tone or contrastive pitch anywhere (a full-text search for stress/accent tone/tonal/pitch: only non-linguistic uses). Stress-only remark; listed as a read-and-dry phonology pointer, not a tone source.
